# Scope and Objections {#sec-scope-objections}

Three scope concessions and two challenges to the result's adequacy. The
missing one — O2, whether the framework *derives* practice's trust
anchors or merely relabels them — is answered as a result rather than
defended as an objection (@sec-introduction, @sec-cell-table).

**Locus, not degree (O1).** This paper formalizes *where* verification
fails and *why*, in three exhaustive cases. It does not formalize how
much trust a failure costs: a single admitted signer and a globally
corrupt certificate authority sit in the same determination-failure
cell, distinguished only by how badly the admitted trust can be abused —
a question this model does not ask.

**Reliance-structure, not trust-proper (O3).** What is formalized is the
structural precondition for trust — an unverifiable gap something must
fill — not trust as the psychological or social attitude the
philosophy-of-trust literature studies (@sec-related-work). This is
conceded ground: the *reliance* a rational agent is forced into once
verification is exhausted is necessary for trust in that fuller sense,
not identical to it.

**Necessary versus elective trust (O4).** The trichotomy characterizes
trust that is *forced* — no scheme exists, at any stratum, for the claim
in question. It says nothing about *elective* trust, where a verifier
could check but chooses reliance for cost or convenience; only the
forced kind is this paper's object.

## Model adequacy (W1)

The sharpest exposure of a result this abstract is whether its
definitions are the right ones. The argument is convergent validity on
three independent prongs.

First, each definition has an independently-adequate home outside this
paper: monotonicity's upward-closed outcomes are CALM's monotone
specifications [@ameloot-neven-vandenbussche-2013; @hellerstein-2026];
certifiability's semi-decidable
class is synthetic topology's affirmable properties [@escardo-2004];
determination, given a mechanism, is the finding archival diplomatics
reports from case-study evidence [@interpares-2002]. Three fields that
do not cite one another arrived at these conditions for their own
reasons.

Second, the instances bite on real systems — most concretely the
split-view reduction of @sec-instances, which predicts a transparency
log's actual deployed defenses rather than classifying the attack after
the fact.

Third, the framework *derives* rather than accommodates: that a failed
axis names a specific anchor — signer, voucher, witness quorum —
recovers the inventory deployed practice converged on by other means,
which is not a check definitions can be tuned to pass.

## Does the factoring distinguish anything? (W2)

Two suspicions attach to any three-way split. The first is that it is a
taxonomy wearing a theorem's clothes: categories somebody chose, with
exhaustiveness asserted once the choosing is done. Here the count runs
the other way — the $\Leftarrow$ leg of $\TTsnap$/$\TTend$ *constructs* a
scheme out of the three conditions, so exhaustiveness follows from what
a scheme is rather than from how the cases were drawn. A taxonomy whose
exhaustiveness is proved is a fair description of this result, and the
proof is what separates it from one merely proposed.

The second suspicion is harder: that the three causes collapse under
pressure, since following any of them far enough lands you in the same
place, trusting the machine in front of you. The cell table
(@sec-cell-table) is the exhibit against that. Three claims, all *above*
the floor — binding
commitments and a faithful verifier already granted — fail on three
different axes and take three visibly different repairs.

**T1, determination.** "The entry at position $k$ was authored by
principal $A$." Authorship is a fact about key custody, which is
context, not bytes; the gate of @sec-theorem fires and no scheme exists
at any stratum. Such claims provably exist
(`Witness.Cells.exists_undetermined_monotone`); reading any *particular*
genuineness or binding claim as one of them is an explicit modeling
hypothesis about the fiber over the record, never a theorem. **Cure:**
admit a witness of history — a signer or attestor whose say-so stands in
for what the record cannot settle.

**T2, certifiability.** "The generator committed at the current head is
degenerate" — that a build emits from a finite table rather than
computing its output. The claim is fixed by the committed bytes,
independent of how the generator is written
(`Witness.Generator.degenerate`, `degenerate_extensional`), and monotone,
since a committed generator stays committed. It is not semi-decidable: a
semantic property of an unbounded-domain denotation, which Rice–Shapiro
places outside $\Sigma_1$ — cited mathematics, not mechanized here.
**Cure:** admit a voucher, a party's judgment standing in for a check no
procedure can perform, or restrict to a decidable subclass.

**T3, monotonicity.** "Entry $e$ is absent from the record,"
equivalently "$w$ is the current head." Determined, certifiable, and
refuted by the next append
(`Witness.Cells.absenceClaim_not_monotone`). **Cure:** admit a holder of
liveness on the present — a witness quorum or gossip protocol — or
restrict to "absent as of time $t$," or accept an expiry window.

Three kinds of party, and three failure modes when the cure is
misplaced: a bad signer yields forged history, a bad voucher a laundered
artifact whose record is nonetheless perfectly consistent, a bad
liveness holder a stale but genuine view. The remaining inhabited cells
compose these failures, and their cures compose too.

None of the three is "trust your CPU." That assumption is real and this
paper names it — it is one of @sec-floor's two residuals, which the
trichotomy sits strictly above by construction. The objection conflates
the floor with the factoring. The floor is where hardware and toolchain
trust lives, it is bounded at two items, and above it the three causes
remain distinct.

## Coverage of the prior-art sweep

The sweep behind @sec-related-work reached arXiv, open bibliographic
indices, author-hosted PDFs, institutional repositories, and the
Internet Archive; paywalled philosophy-of-trust archives, publisher
search interfaces, and rate-limiting citation-graph APIs stayed out of
reach. Post-2022 philosophy-of-trust literature is therefore effectively
unsampled, and several negative findings rest on an
exhaustive check of *one document each*, which closes that document and
not the literature around it. The composition claim is therefore
access-bounded throughout — composed nowhere this sweep could reach,
never a clean-room negative — and @sec-related-work makes the case
positively instead, from what the field demonstrably *did* do.
